title: Katakana M-Row — マ ミ ム メ モ

points.name: マ
points.explanation: マ makes the same 'ma' sound as hiragana ま. Visually, マ has three strokes and looks like a combination of 'T' and a diagonal — a horizontal stroke at top, a shorter horizontal below-left, and a diagonal sweeping to the lower right. Some learners see マ as looking like the Roman letter 'M' simplified into three key strokes, which helps connect the visual to the sound. マ appears in マクドナルド (McDonald's — notice how Japanese adapts this!), マスク (mask), and マーケット (market). マクドナルド is a great example of how Japanese renders foreign names phonetically.
rules: Same 'ma' as ま — both lips close for 'm', then open to 'ah'.
マ has three strokes — can be remembered as a simplified 'M' shape.
マスク (mask) became extremely common vocabulary after 2020.
points.flashcardAnswer: ma — same sound as ま; looks like a simplified 'M'

points.name: ミ
points.explanation: ミ makes the same 'mi' sound as hiragana み. Visually, ミ consists of three parallel horizontal strokes — the top two are shorter and equal length, the bottom one is longer. It resembles the Roman numeral 'III' or a set of stacked lines. Some learners think of ミ as three 'mi' lines, using the repetition to remember the character. Compare to hiragana み, which has a looping, cursive structure. ミ appears in ミルク (milk), ミュージック (music — ミュ is a combination), and ミックス (mix).
rules: ミ = three horizontal strokes (top two shorter, bottom one longer). Like Roman numeral III.
ミュージック (music) uses the ミュ combination — ミ + small ュ = 'myu'.

examples.english: ice cream (ミ in クリーム)

points.flashcardAnswer: mi — same sound as み; looks like three horizontal strokes (III)

points.name: ム
points.explanation: ム makes the same 'mu' sound as hiragana む. Visually, ム is a distinctive character with two strokes: a horizontal line and then a diagonal going lower-left that curves at the bottom and extends to the right. Some describe ム as looking like a shoe or a hooked shape that resembles the number '4' written in a particular way. Compare to hiragana む, which is much more complex with a looping top-right element. ム appears in ムード (mood), ムービー (movie — though 映画[えいが]/えいが is more standard), and in many musical and media terms.
rules: Same 'mu' as む — 'm' + flat, unrounded Japanese 'u'.
ム has two strokes: horizontal line + downward hook curving right.
ム is less common in everyday loanwords than other M-row katakana.
points.flashcardAnswer: mu — same sound as む; looks like a hooked stroke with a horizontal top

points.name: メ
points.explanation: メ makes the same 'me' sound as hiragana め. Visually, メ is straightforward — two diagonal strokes forming an 'X' shape, but with the crossing point higher than center, giving it an asymmetric look. Some see it as an 'X' or a crossed pair of legs. This is quite different from hiragana め, which has a looping structure. メ appears in メール (email / mail), メニュー (menu), and メロン (melon). メール is one of the most essential modern vocabulary words since email communication is ubiquitous.
rules: メ looks like an 'X' with the crossing point toward the top.
メール (email/mail) is essential modern vocabulary — used for both physical mail and email in Japan.
points.flashcardAnswer: me — same sound as め; looks like an 'X' with crossing near the top

points.name: モ
points.explanation: モ makes the same 'mo' sound as hiragana も. Visually, モ looks like a simplified Roman letter 'E' or a backwards '3' — three horizontal strokes with the middle one extending further right, and a vertical connecting them on the left. Compare to hiragana も, which has a hook-like structure with two horizontal strokes. モ appears in モデル (model), モーター (motor), and モーニング (morning — used especially for a Japanese 'morning set' at a coffee shop). モーニング refers to the breakfast set deal many cafes and family restaurants offer.
rules: モ looks like a backwards '3' or a capital 'E' — three horizontal strokes on a vertical.
モーニング (morning set at a café) is a wonderful uniquely Japanese cultural institution.

examples.english: morning / morning set meal at a café

points.flashcardAnswer: mo — same sound as も; looks like a backwards '3' or capital 'E'

chapterPractice.prompt: What sound does this katakana make?
chapterPractice.explanation: メ makes the 'me' sound — same as hiragana め. It looks like an 'X' with the crossing point near the top. メール (email) is one of the most practical words using メ.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which hiragana matches the katakana ミ?
chapterPractice.explanation: ミ and み both make the 'mi' sound. Katakana ミ looks like three horizontal strokes (like Roman numeral III), while hiragana み has a flowing looping structure.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: メニュー (menyuu) means 'menu'. メ (me) + ニュ (nyu, combination) + ー (long u) = menyuu. You'll need to ask for the メニューをください (Please give me the menu) at every restaurant in Japan!

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: マスク (masuku) means 'mask' — a face covering. マ (ma) + ス (su) + ク (ku) = masuku. This word became extremely prominent in everyday Japanese vocabulary.
